analysis.one_liner: Offers House candidates full public campaign financing in exchange for refusing private campaign money.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote in any of the four committees it was sent to, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a voluntary public financing system for House elections. Candidates who collected a set number of $5 contributions from voters in their state could certify as "clean money" candidates, give up private campaign contributions, and receive public funds instead, with extra "fair fight" money if a privately funded opponent or outside groups outspent them. It also would have given those candidates free and discounted broadcast time, capped what political parties could spend in coordination with them, and barred most taxpayer-funded congressional mass mailings in the 90 days before an election.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates for the House without personal wealth or access to wealthy donor networks, including challengers, ordinary citizens considering a run, and minor-party candidates. Voters benefit from less candidate time spent fundraising, more competitive races, and lower-cost campaign ads. Taxpayers could voluntarily donate to the fund and claim a tax credit of up to $500.

how_it_helps.text: A candidate who collects 1,500 qualifying $5 contributions from state residents becomes certified and receives public allocations instead of private contributions, removing dependence on large donors for major-party candidates [S3].

Participating candidates receive 'fair fight' funds matching opposing spending above their allocation, including independent expenditures and electioneering communications, capped at 200% of their allocation, so heavy outside spending cannot drown out a publicly funded candidate [S3].

Clean money candidates are entitled to free broadcast time in prime windows (30 minutes in the primary, 75 minutes in the general) and ad rates capped at 50% of the lowest unit rate, lowering the cost of reaching voters [S3].

Nonparticipating candidates facing a clean candidate face faster and more frequent disclosure of their money, with 48-hour reports once spending crosses a threshold and penalties tied to the fair-fund amounts withheld [S3].

Members of Congress would be barred from sending franked (taxpayer-funded) mass mailings in the 90 days before a primary through the general election, closing a window in which incumbents can reach voters at public expense [S3].

Coordinated spending by political party committees with a participating candidate is capped at the lesser of 10% of the candidate's public allocation, and coordinated payments are treated as contributions, limiting a party-money end run around the system [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the House Clean Elections Fund through appropriations, and donors can claim a tax credit up to $500 for contributions. Broadcast stations bear the cost of mandatory free airtime and half-price ad rates for participating candidates, and the Treasury forgoes the tax credit revenue.

drawbacks.text: The fund is authorized at 'such sums as are necessary' with no cost cap, so the total taxpayer price depends on how many candidates opt in; the up-to-$500 tax credit also forgoes federal revenue [S3].

Minor-party and independent candidates must gather 150% of the qualifying contributions a major-party candidate needs, making the system harder for them to enter even though it is sold as broadening access [S3].

Participating candidates give up private fundraising, so a wealthy self-funding opponent could still spend freely; the bill relies on fair-fight matching funds and rapid reporting to offset that, a mechanism that has been challenged and tightened in state versions of the same system [S3].

Mandating free broadcast time and capping ad rates imposes a direct cost on broadcasters and was likely to draw First Amendment objections; the bill includes special Supreme Court review provisions anticipating constitutional challenges [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a modest, partly voluntary public expenditure (seeded by tax-deductible donations plus appropriations, likely a rounding error next to what skewed legislative outcomes cost) in exchange for severing candidates' dependence on large private checks. The design is not airtight — wealthy self-funders can still outspend a participating candidate, minor parties face a higher qualifying bar, and the free-airtime mandate would have faced court challenges — but the bill acknowledges those weak points with matching funds, audits, and expedited review. As introduced, it is a genuine, fairly engineered attempt at public financing rather than a shell.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four committees on the day it was introduced, bounced to a telecommunications subcommittee the next day, and no committee ever held a hearing, marked it up, or voted on it, so it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the bill on March 20, 2007, joined by Reps. Grijalva and Platts, and it was sent to four committees the same day: House Administration, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Oversight and Government Reform [S3][S5].
The day after introduction, it was referred to the Telecommunications and Internet Subcommittee; that is the last recorded action the bill ever received [S5].

The bill attracted 56 cosponsors — 55 Democrats and 1 Republican — but none of the four committees with jurisdiction ever reported it, and it received no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4][S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the large donors who finance their campaigns are better off, because the privately funded system the bill would have replaced stayed in place untouched. Broadcasters also avoided the free-airtime and rate mandates.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the party split shows only in sponsorship: 55 of the 56 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican, and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would have required stations to give clean-money candidates free prime-time airtime (capped at 15 minutes per station), sell their ads at 50% of the lowest rate, disclose rate cards, and generally not preempt paid candidate ads. That cost to broadcasters is precisely the public's savings on political airtime.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and moneyed interests
industries.note: The bill's findings state outright that private contributions from interests affected by legislation create conflicts and skew legislative outcomes, and the system was designed to replace that money with small $5 voter contributions. Donors whose influence depends on financing campaigns would have lost that channel for participating candidates.

Incumbents benefit most from the existing system — donor networks skew to incumbents and the bill's own findings say so — and the bill would have also barred franked mass mailings in the 90 days before elections. The bill offered incumbents a voluntary opt-in, so nothing compelled them to give up the current arrangement.

Coordinated spending by party committees with a publicly funded candidate would have been cut to no more than 10% of the candidate's public allocation, and coordinated payments treated as contributions, reducing one channel of party money into House races.
